ta-l1d20q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 20, where Lombard proves the persons' equality in power through Augustine. From authority: if the Son had less power than the Father, he would not have all the Father has, but he has all (John 17). Two heretical replies are refuted: that the Son has everything the Father has but not as much of each, since the Son has omnipotence because the Father does; and that the Father is more powerful because he gave the Son power, since he gave either equal power, making the Son omnipotent, or unequal, contradicting that the Son has all. From reason: if the Father begot a Son less powerful, either he could beget an equal and would not, which is envy, or would and could not, which is lack of omnipotence, both impossible; a likeness from human generation confirms this. Finally the reply that the Father is greater because he is begotten of none is refuted, since equality and inequality follow quantity, not relation, and being from the Father signifies only a relation of origin. Three articles are announced: whether the Son is omnipotent, whether he is equal to the Father in omnipotence, and whether there is any order between Father and Son.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father in power, since he has all the Father has.
A Father who could beget an equal Son and did not would be envious; one who could not would not be omnipotent.
Equality follows quantity, not relation of origin.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e137.summary: First argument that the Son is not omnipotent. Power concerns ability for a work (Dist. 7), and there is an operation belonging to the Father's omnipotence that the Son cannot do, active generation.
claims: The Son cannot beget.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e140.summary: Second argument. God is called omnipotent because he can do everything simply possible, and the Father's greatest power is shown in begetting the Son, which is infinitely greater than creating heaven and earth. Since this power is denied to the Son, he is not omnipotent.
claims: Begetting the Son is the Father's greatest power.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e143.summary: Anticipates the reply that the power to beget is not something but toward something, so the Son can do everything though he cannot beget. 'Everything' includes all beings universally, and relatives are among beings, so the distribution covers relatives too.
claims: Relatives are included among all beings.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e147.summary: Anticipates the reply that omnipotence concerns only creatures, not what is in God. Then Augustine's argument in the text would fail, since he argues that if the Father could not beget an equal Son he would not be omnipotent, so the Father's omnipotence extends to the Son's generation, which the Son cannot do.
claims: Augustine's argument requires omnipotence to extend to generation.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e150.summary: Sed contra from the Creed: the Father is omnipotent, the Son omnipotent, the Holy Spirit omnipotent.
claims: The Creed calls each person omnipotent.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e156.summary: Thomas's determination. Without doubt the Son of God is omnipotent as the Father is, though the Son cannot beget. God is called omnipotent because he can do everything, whatever is something or a being. But a relation is 'something' differently from other beings. Other beings are something both in their being and in the concept of their quiddity: wisdom by its being posits something in the subject and by its concept posits a nature in the genus of quality. A relation is something by the being it has in the subject, but by its concept it is not something, only toward another, so by its concept it posits nothing in the subject. Hence Boethius says relatives predicate nothing of what they are said of, and there are things related by a merely conceptual relation that posit nothing real, as the knowable is related to knowledge. This holds of relations in God and in creatures, but differently: a created relation has a being other than its subject's and so is something other than the subject, while in God nothing has a being other than God; wisdom's being is the divine being itself, not added, and likewise paternity's. So a relation, by its being, by which alone it posits something, is the divine essence, and by its concept, by which it distinguishes one person from another, it is not something but toward something. So although the Father has paternity, which the Son lacks, and paternity is something, the Father has nothing the Son lacks: paternity is the essence and the Son lacks paternity, but it does not follow that the Father has any essence the Son lacks. If the Father had wisdom and the Son did not, the Father would have something the Son lacks, since wisdom posits something even by its concept. Likewise, since begetting in God is a relation and is something, although the Father can beget and the Son cannot, it does not follow that the Father can do something the Son cannot. It would follow if the Father could understand and the Son could not. As the Father is Father and being Father is being something, yet since the Son is not Father, there is no being of the Father that is not the Son's, since all being in God is the essence's.
claims: The Son is omnipotent although he cannot beget.
A relation posits something only by its being, which in God is the essence; by its concept it is only toward another.
So the Father, though he has paternity and can beget, has and can do nothing that the Son lacks.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the first argument. Generation signifies a relation by way of operation and is also an operation of the divine nature (Damascene). Although generation does not belong to the Son, it does not follow that some operation belongs to the Father that does not belong to the Son: by one and the same operation the Father begets and the Son is born, but it is in Father and Son under different relations.
claims: By one operation the Father begets and the Son is born.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the second argument. No power is taken from the Son; by the same power by which the Father begets, the Son is begotten.
claims: The same power by which the Father begets is that by which the Son is begotten.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e165.summary: Reply to the third argument. Relatives are included in 'everything' as to the being they have, for in this way a relative is something among all things, but not as to the concept of relation by which it is referred to another, since in that way it is not something simply.
claims: Relatives fall under 'everything' only as to their being.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. God's omnipotence can be related to something as to a product or as to an operation. As to a product, it is not related to anything in God, since nothing in God is made, and so omnipotence concerns creatures only. As to operation, it is related to what is in him, especially since none of his operations is outside his essence. So the Father's omnipotence extends to begetting, understanding, creating, and in short to everything pertaining to perfection, and Augustine's argument is effective. Yet it does not follow that the Son is not omnipotent if he cannot beget an equal Son, for the reason given. It would follow for the Father, since he does not lack the relation signified in active generation, so if the perfection of generation were denied him there would be a defect in the operation as operation, which would redound to a defect of power. Active generation is removed from the Son only by reason of the relation it implies, and relation as such has no order to power (Dist. 2).
claims: Omnipotence extends to God's internal operations, including generation, as operations.
The Son's not begetting is no defect of power, since it is removed from him only by reason of relation, which has no order to power.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e181.summary: First argument that the Son is not equal to the Father in omnipotence. Power is appropriated to the Father, not the Son (Dist. 31), so it belongs more to the Father.
claims: Power is appropriated to the Father.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e184.summary: Second argument. Between having something from another personally and essentially (as creatures do) and having nothing from another either way (as the Father does), there is a middle: having from another personally but not essentially, as the Son does. The extremes signify dignity and authority, and diminishment and defect, and a middle shares the nature of the extremes, so the Son has something of dignity (not having essentially from another) and something of defect (having personally from another), and is less powerful.
claims: The Son is a middle between the Father and creatures in receiving from another.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e187.summary: Third argument. In creatures nothing received from another is as powerful as its source, as light in the air is not as powerful as light in the sun. The Son's power is received from the Father.
claims: What is received is less than its source.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument. What acts through another seems more powerful than that through which it acts, and the Father acts through the Son and not conversely.
claims: What acts through another is more powerful.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e194.summary: Sed contra, which is granted. Power is rooted in essence, and Father and Son have numerically one essence, so one power, and there is no inequality in power, since every inequality implies diversity: as one in quantity makes equal, diverse makes unequal.
claims: Numerically one essence entails one power and so equality of power.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e197.summary: Reply to the first argument. Power is appropriated to the Father not because it belongs to him more than to the Son but because it resembles his property more than the Son's: power has the character of principle, and the Father is the principle without principle.
claims: Power is appropriated to the Father because it resembles his property as principle without principle.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e200.summary: Reply to the second argument. Having from another essentially and personally implies defect only in having from another essentially, i.e. in diversity of essence, which causes inequality of magnitude and potentiality, since diversity causes inequality as unity causes equality. In this respect the Son is not a middle between the Father and creatures; not having from another essentially belongs to the Son with the same and equal dignity as to the Father.
claims: Defect arises only from receiving a diverse essence; the Son shares the Father's essence and dignity equally.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the third argument. In lower things something is sometimes received with the same power as in its source, when the recipient is proportioned to receive the whole power of the giver, as in all univocal generation, when man begets man and fire fire. Sometimes the whole power is not received, from a defect of the recipient, not proportioned to receive all the agent can give, as lower bodies are to the sun's action, or perhaps from a defect of the agent, whose power falls short of communicating its likeness, as one spark cannot heat a log however disposed. In God there is no defect on either side, the power of both being one and the same, so the Son receives from the Father as much power as the Father has.
claims: In God neither giver nor receiver is defective, so the Son receives the Father's whole power.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. When the Father is said to act through the Son, no degree of power is posited, only authority in the Father (Dist. 15).
claims: 'Through the Son' signifies the Father's authority, not greater power.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e223.summary: First argument that there is no order among the divine persons. Augustine defines order as the disposition of equal and unequal things assigning each its place, and no local disposition fits the divine persons.
claims: Augustine defines order by place.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e226.summary: Second argument from Boethius: difference of deity follows those who posit grades in the Trinity. Wherever there is order there is some grade, so order among the persons would imply diversity of deity.
claims: Grades in the Trinity would imply diversity of deity.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e232.summary: Third argument. Where eternity, simplicity, and dignity are the same there is no order: equal eternity excludes temporal order, equal simplicity excludes the order of cause and effect and of part and whole, and equal dignity excludes order of dignity. Father and Son have numerically the same eternity, simplicity, and dignity.
claims: Same eternity, simplicity, and dignity exclude every order.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e235.summary: Fourth argument. Whatever is in God signifies either the essence or a notion. Order does not pertain to the essence, which has no distinction, nor to a notion, since no notion is common to the three persons as order is.
claims: Order is neither essential nor notional.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e239.summary: Sed contra. Wherever there is plurality without order there is confusion, and in the divine persons there is plurality but no confusion, so there is order.
claims: Plurality without order is confusion.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e242.summary: Second sed contra. The Spirit is called the third person in the Trinity, which implies some order.
claims: 'Third person' implies order.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e251.summary: Further question: whether there is an order of nature. It seems not, since all order implies distinction, there is no distinction in the divine nature, so there is no order of the nature and no order of nature among the persons.
claims: The divine nature has no distinction.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e254.summary: Second argument. The divine nature is the same as the essence, and it is nonsense to speak of an order of essence among the persons, so neither of nature.
claims: Nature and essence are the same.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e266.summary: Thomas's answer to the first sub-question. Order in its concept includes three things: the character of prior and posterior, so there can be order according to every way in which something is called prior to another, in place, in time, and so on; distinction, since order is only of distinct things, though the name presupposes this more than it signifies it; and the ground of the order, by which order is specified, so that there is order of place, of dignity, of origin, and so on. The order of origin belongs to the divine persons. 'Order of nature' signifies the order of origin, taking 'nature' as the Philosopher does (Metaphysics 5), as that from which what sprouts first sprouts, so 'nature' implies origin, and 'order of nature' functions as one name signifying a species of order. This species is preserved in the divine persons by its differentia, origin, not by its genus, priority and posteriority, as with many other things. Augustine's definition shows this: the order of nature is that by which one is from another, which posits the differentia of origin, and not prior to another, which removes the generic character. So one should not grant that there is order simply in God, only order of nature.
claims: Order includes priority, distinction, and a specifying ground.
In God there is order of origin ('order of nature') by its differentia, origin, without its genus, priority.
There is not order simply in God, only order of nature.
concepts: genus and differentia in divine names

ta-l1d20q1-d1e269.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine's definition concerns order of place, which does not fit the divine persons.
claims: Augustine's definition concerns local order.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e272.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'Grade' signifies a species of order according to dignity, perfection, or place, none of which fits the divine persons, so neither does grade.
claims: There are no grades among the persons.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e275.summary: Reply to the third argument. It concerns order by its generic character, positing prior and posterior, which in no way fits God.
claims: God admits no priority and posteriority.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e279.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Order' signifies a notion, not in particular but in general, determined by various additions: 'order of Father to Son' signifies paternity, 'order of Son to Father' filiation, and likewise in other cases. The same holds of 'principle', which signifies one notion when the Father is called principle of the Son and another when called principle of the Spirit.
claims: 'Order' and 'principle' signify notions in general, determined by their additions.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e282.summary: Reply to the first sed contra. The order of origin suffices to exclude confusion and for the Spirit to be called the third person.
claims: Order of origin excludes confusion and grounds 'third person'.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e285.summary: The reply to the second sed contra follows from this.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e295.summary: Thomas's answer to the second sub-question. There is an order of nature in God, not in that the nature is ordered or that the Father is naturally prior to the Son, but because 'nature' expresses the ground of the order, as it implies origin. Although the divine nature is really the same as the essence, the concept of origin is not implied in 'essence' as it is in 'nature', since they differ conceptually, so one cannot speak of an order of essence as of an order of nature.
claims: 'Order of nature' is legitimate because 'nature' implies origin; 'order of essence' is not, though nature and essence are really identical.

ta-l1d20q1-d1e309.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Augustine's argument 'if the Son has less in power, not all the Father's things are his' seems to shift from what to how much, arguing 'the Son has all the Father has, so not less power', and the argument from omnipotence seems to make the same error, since omnipotence also names a quantity of power. The argument is not valid by its form but is valid from the nature of the thing argued about: the Son cannot have what the Father has except as numerically the same and unchanged, so as much as is in the Father is in the Son. (2) 'If you say he would not, you call him envious' seems not to follow, since by the same reasoning one could prove that God could not have made any creature better than he did. The cases differ: denying a thing what is due to it is envy, but not giving what is not due is not. Equality with the begetter is due to the Son by the nature of deity, so withholding it would be envy, whereas no creature is due by nature more perfection than follows from its natural principles, so what is added to rational nature is attributed to grace and can be withheld without envy. (3) 'Equality of what kind or how great' seems false, since unity of quality causes likeness, not equality (the Philosopher). In God equality follows only quantity of power, which is founded on quality, so equality is said to follow quality.
claims: Augustine's argument holds because the Son has what the Father has as numerically identical.
Withholding what is due is envy; equality is due to the Son by nature, but superadded perfection to creatures is grace.
In God equality follows quantity of power founded on quality.
concepts: numerical identity of the divine nature

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e218.summary: Sub-question 1 states arguments against any order among the divine persons, from Augustine's local definition, Boethius on grades, the identity of eternity, simplicity, and dignity, and the dichotomy of essence and notion, against arguments from the absence of confusion and from 'third person'.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e246.summary: Sub-question 2 asks whether there is an order of nature, given that the divine nature has no distinction and is the same as the essence.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e261.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 1 holds that order includes priority, distinction, and a specifying ground. In God there is order of origin, 'order of nature', by its differentia, origin, without its genus, priority, so there is not order simply, only order of nature. 'Order' and 'principle' signify notions in general, and order of origin excludes confusion and grounds the Spirit's being third person.
claims: In God there is order of origin without priority; not order simply.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e290.summary: Thomas's answer to sub-question 2 holds that there is an 'order of nature' because 'nature' implies origin. One cannot say 'order of essence', since 'essence' does not imply origin, though essence and nature are really identical.
claims: 'Order of nature' is said, not 'order of essence'.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 20 maps Augustine's proofs of the persons' equality in power from authority and reason, the dilemma of envy or impotence, and the reply that relation of origin does not cause inequality. It announces articles on the Son's omnipotence, his equality in it, and order among the persons.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father in power.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e129.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Son is omnipotent. Thomas holds that he is, though he cannot beget. A relation posits something only by its being, which in God is the divine essence, and by its concept it is only toward another. So the Father, though he has paternity and can beget, has and can do nothing the Son lacks, as he would if he alone could understand. Father and Son share one operation and one power under different relations. Omnipotence extends to God's internal operations as operations, and the Son's not begetting is no defect of power, since relation has no order to power.
claims: The Son is omnipotent; not begetting is no defect of power, because relations posit nothing beyond the essence.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e173.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Son is equal to the Father in omnipotence. Thomas grants it: one essence means one power and so equality. Power is appropriated to the Father only by likeness to his property as principle without principle. Defect arises only from receiving a diverse essence, which the Son does not. In God neither giver nor receiver is defective, so the Son receives the Father's whole power, and 'through the Son' signifies authority, not greater power.
claims: The Son is equal to the Father in power, sharing numerically one essence and power.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e210.summary: Article 3 asks whether there is order between Father and Son. Thomas holds that there is an order of nature, that is of origin, signified by the differentia of order without its generic priority. There is not order simply or any grade, and the order is not of the essence, since 'nature' implies origin while 'essence' does not.
claims: There is an order of nature (origin) without priority among the persons.

ta-l1d20q1-Dd1e304.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 20 defends Augustine's argument from the numerical identity of what the Son receives. It distinguishes the envy of withholding what is due, equality being due to the Son, from God's free withholding of gratuitous perfection from creatures, and explains equality by quantity of power founded on quality.
claims: Equality is due to the Son by nature; superadded perfection to creatures is grace.

ta-l1d20q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 20 treats the persons' equality in power. Article 1 holds that the Son is omnipotent though he cannot beget. A relation posits something only by its being, which in God is the essence, so the Father's paternity and active generation give him nothing the Son lacks, and not begetting is no defect of power. Article 2 holds that the Son is equal to the Father in omnipotence, sharing numerically one essence and power. Power is appropriated to the Father only by likeness to his property, and in God neither giver nor receiver is defective. Article 3 holds that there is an 'order of nature' among the persons, an order of origin preserved by its differentia without the generic priority of order, so there is neither order simply nor any grade. The Expositio defends Augustine's arguments and distinguishes what is due to the Son by nature from what is given to creatures by grace.
claims: The Son is omnipotent and equal to the Father in power, though he cannot beget.
Relations posit nothing beyond the essence, so not begetting is no defect of power.
Among the persons there is order of origin without priority or grade.
